correctness.rationale: Farhi–Kane gives omission of the full p-power p^a in L_k exactly when v_p(k+1)≥a=floor(log_p k), with at most one omitted prime. For N=k+1 this gives N=mp^a with 2≤m≤p: k≥p^a excludes m=1, and k<p^(a+1) gives m≤p. Conversely these inequalities ensure the exact defect exponent. For a=1 the prime p≥m is the unique largest prime factor at least sqrt(N), including equality for squares. For each a≥2, split the higher-power count at B=Y^(1/(a+1)); summing p below B and Y/p^a above B over all integers gives O(B²) with a uniform constant for a≥2 by the integral tail. Summing exponents gives O(Y^(2/3) log Y), negligible against Y/log²Y. The reindexing Y=X+1 changes the centered count by O(1); p dividing fixed q contributes only finitely many exponent-one pairs. The cofactor weight w_q has O(q) partial sums, so the lower endpoint subtraction π(m-1) costs O_q(sqrt(X)). The effective prime number theorem works uniformly for X/m≥sqrt(X); summing individual errors costs at most a logarithmic factor before the exponential saving. Li(t)-t/log t has derivative 1/log²t, and Abel summation bounds its weighted contribution by O_q(X/log²X). For the last Taylor remainder, write u=log m and L=log X: the logarithmic derivative of u exp(-u)/(L-u) is 1/u-1+1/(L-u), nonincreasing for u≤L/2. Thus this factor has supremum and variation O(1/L), giving the required second Abel bound. The centered harmonic tail converges by bounded partial sums. Möbius inclusion–exclusion gives the local logarithmic divisor sum; subtracting w_q(1) is essential because primes are not defects. This yields C_2=(log 2-1)/2<0 and C_3=(log 3-1)/3>0. The unweighted leading integral between m=2 and sqrt(X) is log 2+O(1/log X), and the total effect of the π(m-1) terms there is O(X/log X). Independently, cyclically comparing quotient samples modulo L_k gave the predicted least periods for k=1 through 8; a separate smallest-prime-factor sieve applying the pointwise formula to k≤300000 gave 195365 defects, split 193988 and 1377, and normalized centered counts -0.175111 and +0.035803 for q=2,3 at that bound. Replay by direct quotient evaluation over a full period for the small cases and factorization of k+1 for the larger diagnostic. The frozen verify.py was inspected, not executed. Neither finite check proves the asymptotic. The theorem fixes q in advance.

evidence: Hildebrand–Tenenbaum's precise de Bruijn approximation (attributed to Saias) applies uniformly for x=X/d and y=sqrt(X), including u near 2 from below, with a remainder smaller than x/log²y. Granville reports the familiar two-term expansion.

For X large every d dividing fixed q is y-smooth, so Ψ_q(X,y)=Σ_{d|q} μ(d) Ψ(X/d,y). Taylor expansion at u=2 of the common-cutoff approximation gives a d-dependent term (X/d) log d/log X because ρ'(2)=-1/2; the common lower-order term cancels in Ψ_q-(φ(q)/q)Ψ. Thus the centered fixed-cutoff smooth coefficient is Σ μ(d)log(d)/d, and complementing it reverses its sign.
The smooth-number progression results of Harper, Soundararajan and the Cambridge article normalize by Ψ_q/φ(q); they do not by themselves supply the total coprimality correction.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The uniform unweighted expansion is stronger than a first-order Dickman estimate and actually yields the analytic coefficient for the fixed-threshold proxy. To see the requisite uniformity from (1.29), subtract the unit step from floor(v)/v in its Stieltjes integral. Integration by parts yields a first correction proportional to ρ'(u)/log y; the remaining integral is O(log^-2 y) near u=2 because floor(v)/v-1=O(1/v), the log moment in the differentiated integral is integrable, and ρ' is Lipschitz near 2. Its exact common coefficient cancels. Transferring this proxy to the moving composite threshold and then to actual period defects requires the separate arithmetic estimates; the inspected smooth-number statements do not make that transfer.

originality.rationale: The fixed-window period criterion and the leading largest-prime-factor density are prior. Moreover the classical uniform smooth-number expansion gives the fixed-cutoff coprimality coefficient by inclusion–exclusion; that analytic coefficient in isolation is not a new smooth-number phenomenon. What remains is the arithmetic reduction linking the actual least-period defect at its moving cutoff to that coefficient at the stated error scale, excluding the prime layer and controlling higher omitted powers. This produces an explicit sign-changing second-order law for the original period statistic. The bounded comparison did not establish earlier coverage of this reduction or frequency law. It is not publication-priority clearance.
residual_risks: Earlier work on centered largest-prime-factor counts at a varying threshold, or on frequencies of Farhi–Kane exceptions, could already contain the substantive reduction or the law. The comparison does not exclude unindexed results.
The original Saias article was not independently obtained; the Hildebrand–Tenenbaum statement is the checked precise uniform approximation. Other cited full papers were not all read in full.
Nearby fixed-cutoff smooth-number asymptotics genuinely account for the corresponding local coefficient after Möbius summation; originality should not be attributed to that proxy calculation alone.

value.rationale: A fixed-k exact period formula does not quantify how frequently its full period fails over k, or how coprimality affects that frequency. The leading share hides a signed correction which changes direction even for the two smallest prime moduli. The prime exclusion and suppression of higher omitted powers explain that phenomenon and give a usable second-order benchmark for this natural period statistic. The significance is the centered period law, not a new general smooth-number asymptotic or the finite sieve data.
